960.title: Aryadeva
960.hook: Nagarjuna's student, who carried the middle way on
960.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, Aryadeva's Four Hundred verses are studied alongside Nagarjuna's works in the Madhyamaka curriculum, and teachers explain its verse on the order of teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Suhrllekha, Nagarjuna's Letter to a Friend, to be honored like a Buddha carved from plain wood.

A great teacher is only half of a lineage. The other half is the person who listens closely enough to carry it after the teacher is gone. Nagarjuna had such a student: Aryadeva. Tradition remembers him less for inventing a new idea than for taking his teacher's middle way out into the world and testing it, in debate halls, against rival schools, and in verses of his own.
screen: `HALF OF A LINEAGE.` → `ARYADEVA, THE STUDENT.` → `TAKING THE MIDDLE WAY OUT.`

segments.voice: Tradition also calls him Kanadeva, explains the name as the one-eyed deva, and tells a legend to account for it. Someone admired one of his eyes, so he took it out and gave it away, to show that the body isn't worth clinging to. It's a legend, told to make a point about letting go. His book is the Four Hundred, verses that put Nagarjuna's emptiness to work against clinging: to permanence, to the body, to pleasure, to the self. One verse lays out a teacher's order. First turn a student away from harmful actions. Then, in the middle, away from the idea of a solid self. And last, away from every view at all. Even emptiness isn't a place to cling. That's a teacher thinking about how a student actually grows: one step, then the next. Then a hard ending. A Chinese account of his life says a follower of a rival he had beaten in debate attacked him with a knife. As he lay dying, Aryadeva told his own students not to chase the man, and spoke of the attacker with compassion. In that telling, the last thing he taught was the teaching itself, lived. A student who carried it to the end.
screen: `KANADEVA, THE ONE-EYED.` · `THE FOUR HUNDRED VERSES.` · `HARM, THEN SELF, THEN ALL VIEWS.` · `DON'T CHASE HIM.` · then, large: `THE STUDENT CARRIES IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing a teacher showed you, a way of cooking, of fixing something, of calming down, and ask how you do it now. What did you keep exactly as you were shown, and what did you test for yourself and change? Rest there, noticing where you, like Aryadeva, took a teacher's way out into the world.
Aryadeva. Nagarjuna's student, who wrote the Four Hundred verses and, in a Chinese account, forgave the man who struck him down. Today's word.
Your line: the student carries it. Every lineage needs someone listening that closely. Day nine hundred sixty.

961.title: Asanga and the dog
961.hook: after years of failure, Asanga tends a wounded dog and Maitreya appears (a legend)
961.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist teachers tell the story of Asanga and the dog when teaching great compassion, and Asanga is honored in Tibetan tradition as a founder of the lineage of vast activity received from Maitreya.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Aryadeva, Nagarjuna's student, who forgave the man who struck him down. Your line: the student carries it.

A monk sits alone in a cave on a mountain. His name is Asanga, and he has one wish: to see Maitreya, the Buddha who is to come, face to face, and learn from him. He meditates for years. Nothing. He gives up, walks down the mountain, sees something that shames him into trying again, and climbs back up. Years more. Nothing. Again and again. At last, Tibetan tellers say, he leaves for good. On the road down, a dog is lying in the dust.
screen: `A CAVE, AND ONE WISH.` → `YEARS, AND NOTHING.` → `A DOG IN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Each time Asanga quits, he meets a small lesson in patience. A man rubbing an iron bar with a soft cloth, to make a needle. Drops of water that have worn a hollow into stone. Each sends him back up the mountain, and still nothing. On his last walk down he finds the dog, its back half an open wound, crawling with maggots. Something in him breaks open. He wants to help the dog, but he doesn't want to kill the maggots either. So he cuts flesh from his own thigh to give them somewhere to go, then closes his eyes and bends to lift them away with his tongue, so as not to crush them with his fingers. His tongue touches the ground. The dog is gone. Maitreya stands there, shining. Asanga, in tears, asks why he never came in all those years. Maitreya answers that he was always there. What hid him was Asanga's own mind, until great compassion cleared it. To prove it, the story says, Asanga carries Maitreya on his shoulder into the town. Almost no one sees anything; one old woman sees only a dog. It's a legend, and Tibetan teachers tell it as one, with a point. Tradition goes on to credit Asanga with teachings received from Maitreya, the ground of the school we meet in two days. But the story's own lesson is simpler. Effort alone didn't let him see. Compassion opened his eyes.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hurting thing, a wilted plant, a friend who has gone quiet, a sore muscle in your own back, and give it plain attention first, the way Asanga finally looked at the dog. Then let one gentle thing you could do for it come to mind, and rest with that wish.
Maitreya. The Buddha who is to come, whom Asanga saw at last in the place of a wounded dog he had tended. Today's word.
Your line: compassion opened his eyes. Years of effort, and the door was a wounded dog. Until tomorrow.

962.title: Vasubandhu
962.hook: Asanga's brother, who wrote a great summary of the Abhidharma, then turned to "mind only"
962.howItsDone: Vasubandhu's Treasury of Abhidharma is studied in Tibetan monastic colleges and in East Asian Buddhist scholarship, and his later verse works are core texts of the Yogacara school.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asanga and the dog. Compassion cleared his eyes, and Maitreya was there all along.

Asanga had a younger brother: brilliant, sharp in debate, and, at first, not impressed by his older brother's new Mahayana teachings at all. In fact, the old account says, he mocked them. His name was Vasubandhu. Before he was done, he'd write a great handbook of Buddhist thought, and then become a voice for the very teaching he'd laughed at. A clever person who changed his mind in public.
screen: `ASANGA'S YOUNGER BROTHER.` → `HE MOCKED THE NEW TEACHING.` → `THEN HE CHANGED HIS MIND.`

segments.voice: Vasubandhu studied the Abhidharma, the careful lists that break experience into its smallest parts: moments of mind, kinds of feeling, causes and conditions. He gathered it into verses with his own commentary, the Abhidharmakosha, the Treasury of Abhidharma. Here and there in the commentary he quietly disagrees with the school he's summarizing. Even his handbook argues. Then the turn. The Life of Vasubandhu, an old account kept in Chinese, tells it this way. Asanga, worried for his brother, sent word that he was ill. Vasubandhu came. That night he heard a Mahayana sutra being recited, and something in it reached him. He saw he'd been wrong, and he was so ashamed of the words he'd spoken against it that he wanted to cut out his own tongue. Asanga told him no. The tongue that had spoken against the teaching could now speak for it. So Vasubandhu turned to the Mahayana and wrote short, dense verses and commentaries on how the mind shapes what it sees: the teaching called mind only, which opens tomorrow. Some later writers have wondered whether two different men named Vasubandhu lie behind all these books. Tradition remembers one. Either way, the story's lesson stays. He didn't hide his old self. He changed his mind, and put the same sharp tongue to new work.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you once said against a person, a place or an idea, and later saw differently. No need to cut anything out: find one fair, true thing you could say in its favor now, say it silently once, and notice how it sits in the mouth.
Vasubandhu. Asanga's brother, who wrote the Treasury of Abhidharma, mocked the Mahayana, then turned to it and wrote on mind only. Today's word.

963.title: Mind only
963.hook: the Yogacara school: how the mind shapes the world it sees
963.howItsDone: Yogacara texts are studied in Tibetan monastic curricula and in East Asian Buddhism, where the Faxiang school carried them, and their account of mind and seeds shapes how teachers in those traditions explain meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vasubandhu, who mocked the Mahayana and then wrote for it. Your line: he changed his mind.

A dream can hold a street, a house, a stranger who speaks, even a fear that makes the heart race. While it lasts, all of it seems solid and outside. Then you wake, and it was all made by the mind. Vasubandhu, the brother who changed his mind, builds one of his short verse works around exactly this kind of example. He asks: what if waking life is shaped by the mind far more than it seems?
screen: `A DREAM FEELS SOLID.` → `THEN YOU WAKE.` → `WHAT IF WAKING IS SHAPED TOO?`

segments.voice: Tradition explains Yogacara as the practice of yoga, the path of meditators. The school grew from the teachings tradition credits to Asanga and Maitreya, and from Vasubandhu's verses. Its other name is mind only. In his Twenty Verses, Vasubandhu argues that, as in a dream, places and times and other beings can appear vividly with nothing outside the mind behind them. Then a stranger picture. Where people see a river of water, he says, hungry ghosts see a river of pus. Same river, different minds, different worlds. Yogacara teachers also describe a deep layer of mind, the storehouse consciousness, where every action leaves a seed. When a seed ripens, it shapes how the next moment looks. So yesterday's anger tints what you see today. How to read it? Some readers, in India, Tibet and today, take Yogacara to say there's no world outside the mind at all. Others say it describes experience: we never meet the world raw, only as our minds have shaped it, and that's what practice works on. Madhyamaka teachers in Tibet debated Yogacara closely, and Tibetan monastic colleges still study both schools. A much older line, from the Dhammapada in Max Müller's translation, points in a similar direction: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." Yogacara takes that thought its own way. The mind doesn't just react to the world. It colors it.

segments.voice: Pick something in front of you, or a person you'll see later, and notice the color your mind already gives it: pleasant, annoying, boring, dear. Ask where that color came from, a memory, a mood, a habit. You don't have to remove it; just see it as a color laid on top, and look at the thing underneath for a few breaths.

964.title: Buddhist logic
964.hook: Dignaga and Dharmakirti: how we know what we know
964.howItsDone: In Tibetan monasteries, students train in debate built on Dignaga and Dharmakirti's logic, standing and clapping as they challenge a seated opponent, and Dharmakirti's works are a core part of the curriculum.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yogacara, the school of mind only. Your line: the mind colors it.

Smoke is rising over a hill. Nobody can see a flame from here, and yet anyone watching would say, without a second thought, there's a fire up there. How do they know? They didn't see it. They worked it out. That small step, from smoke to fire, became the standard example in a long Indian argument about knowing itself, and Buddhist teachers took part. If the mind colors everything, how can anyone trust what they know?
screen: `SMOKE OVER A HILL.` → `NO FLAME IN SIGHT.` → `HOW DO WE KNOW?`

segments.voice: Indian thinkers of different schools argued over pramana, the valid ways of knowing: what counts as real evidence? Buddhist teachers joined in, because the path depends on seeing things as they are, not as we wish. Dignaga, a Buddhist teacher in the line of Vasubandhu, cut the list down. In his Compendium on Valid Knowledge, he holds that there are two ways of knowing. Perception: the bare meeting with what's in front of you, before words get attached. And inference: reasoning from a sign to what it points to, like smoke to fire. Everything else, he argued, either reduces to these or isn't reliable knowing. A later teacher, Dharmakirti, took Dignaga's work further and sharpened the rules of a good inference. The sign has to really belong to the thing. Smoke shows fire only because smoke can't come without fire. A sign that only sometimes goes with a thing proves nothing. These teachers weren't doing logic for its own sake. They wanted a way to tell real knowing from mere opinion. A verse that later Buddhist writers quote, attributed to the Buddha, asks people to test his words the way a goldsmith tests gold, rather than take them on trust. Their work traveled to Tibet, where monks still practice debate, clapping to drive home each point, in a tradition built on these thinkers.
screen: `PRAMANA: WHAT COUNTS AS KNOWING?` · `DIGNAGA: PERCEPTION AND INFERENCE.` · `DHARMAKIRTI: THE SIGN MUST BELONG.` · `TEST IT LIKE GOLD.` · then, large: `HOW DO YOU KNOW?`

segments.voice: Choose one belief you're fairly sure of right now, that a friend is upset with you, or that you left the stove on, and ask: did I perceive this directly, or infer it from a sign? If it's a sign, does it really belong to the thing, like smoke to fire, or only sometimes go with it? Hold the answer gently, with nothing to fix.
Buddhist logic. The tradition of Dignaga and Dharmakirti: two ways of knowing, perception and inference, and careful rules for telling a good sign from a bad one. Today's word.
Your line: how do you know. A question simple enough for any kitchen table. Day nine hundred sixty-four, complete.

965.title: Buddhaghosa
965.hook: the scholar whose Path of Purification maps the Theravada path
965.howItsDone: Theravada monks and meditation teachers study the Visuddhimagga as a guide to practice, and its account of virtue, concentration and wisdom shapes how the path is taught in Theravada monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Buddhist logic, from smoke to fire. Your line: how do you know.

A scholar from India arrives at the Great Monastery in Sri Lanka. He wants to study the old commentaries kept there, in the island's own language, and put them into Pali. The elders are careful. Before handing over their treasures, they set him a test: a few lines from the Buddha's own words, and, in effect, show us what you understand. His answer, the chronicle says, became a book. His name was Buddhaghosa.
screen: `A SCHOLAR ARRIVES IN SRI LANKA.` → `THE ELDERS SET A TEST.` → `THE ANSWER BECOMES A BOOK.`

segments.voice: In the Samyutta Nikaya, a deity asks the Buddha a riddle. There's a tangle inside and a tangle outside; people are caught in a tangle; who can untangle it? The Buddha answers: a wise person, standing firm in virtue, developing the mind and wisdom, can untangle the tangle. Those are the lines the elders gave. Buddhaghosa's answer was the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification. It takes the three things in the Buddha's reply, virtue, the mind trained in concentration, and wisdom, and builds the whole book around them, in that order. Inside, it lays out the path in practical detail: how to keep precepts, how to choose a meditation subject that suits your temperament, how concentration deepens, and what insight sees. It reads like a guide to the territory. Then a legend with a wink. The chronicle says that when Buddhaghosa finished, the gods hid the book to test him, and he wrote it again. Hidden again, he wrote it a third time. Then the first two reappeared, and when the elders read the three copies side by side, they matched, word for word. Tellers enjoy the story for what it says about him: he didn't need the book to know the path. He had walked it before he mapped it.
screen: `A TANGLE INSIDE, A TANGLE OUTSIDE.` · `VIRTUE, CONCENTRATION, WISDOM.` · `A GUIDE TO THE TERRITORY.` · `THREE COPIES, WORD FOR WORD.` · then, large: `THE PATH MAPPED.`

segments.voice: Hold Buddhaghosa's map in mind, virtue, concentration, wisdom, and ask gently where you're standing on it right now: keeping a promise to yourself, steadying the mind, or seeing something clearly. There's no grade here; just find where you are, and rest there with the breath.
Buddhaghosa. The scholar whose Path of Purification maps the way through virtue, concentration and wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: the path mapped. Virtue, a steadier mind, clearer seeing: three ways through the tangle. See you on the path tomorrow.

966.title: The lazy monk
966.hook: a legend: Shantideva, thought lazy, is asked to recite, and recites a masterpiece
966.howItsDone: Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva is studied and recited in Tibetan Buddhism, and teachers tell the legend of his recitation at Nalanda when introducing the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Buddhaghosa, whose book, written three times, matched word for word. Your line: the path mapped.

A busy house can have one person who never seems to do anything. At the great monastery of Nalanda, the legend says, that person was a young monk named Shantideva. The others saw him eat, sleep and wander, and never study, and tradition says they gave him a teasing nickname for it. So they hatched a plan to embarrass him into leaving: invite him to give a public recitation, in front of everyone, and let him fail.
screen: `A MONK WHO SEEMS TO DO NOTHING.` → `A PLAN TO EMBARRASS HIM.` → `A PUBLIC RECITATION.`

segments.voice: In the Tibetan telling, the monks set up a high teaching seat, some say on purpose without steps, and gathered a crowd. Shantideva arrived, settled onto the seat without trouble, and asked a calm question. Shall I recite something old, or something new? They asked for something new, expecting nothing. And he began the Bodhicharyavatara, the Way of the Bodhisattva: verses on the joy of the awakening mind, on patience, on effort, on meditation, on wisdom. The crowd went quiet. The lazy one spoke, and out came a masterpiece. Then the vanishing. The legend says that when he reached the chapter on wisdom, at the verse where neither something nor nothing remains before the mind, he rose into the air and disappeared from sight, while his voice went on reciting. His work was gathered afterward from those who had heard it. Nobody had known what was going on inside him. Quiet isn't the same as empty. And that fits the week behind us. Aryadeva, the student who carried it. Asanga, whose eyes compassion opened. Vasubandhu, who changed his mind. Yogacara and the mind that colors everything. Logic asking how you know. Buddhaghosa's map. And now a monk everyone had judged, wrongly. Tomorrow, one of his teachings.
screen: `A HIGH SEAT, A CROWD.` · `SOMETHING OLD, OR SOMETHING NEW?` · `HE RISES, AND HIS VOICE GOES ON.` · `QUIET IS NOT EMPTY.` · then, large: `THE LAZY ONE SPOKE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you may have quietly written off, a coworker who seems checked out, a relative who never says much, and picture them with whole rooms inside them that you've never seen. Then let one small, kind surprise for them take shape, a thank-you, a real question, a bit of help, and rest with it.
Shantideva. The monk at Nalanda judged idle, who stood up and recited the Way of the Bodhisattva. Today's word.
Your line: the lazy one spoke. There may be a masterpiece you just haven't heard yet. That's the week, done.
